thesis: Passion, compulsive use and psychosis are distinct, not inevitable stages.

ideas.statement: Evaluate certainty, revisability and consequences without diagnosing unusual ideas.
Respect persons without affirming unsupported beliefs and recognize professional assessment needs.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: One person works late on an idea. Another talks to a chatbot daily. A third is convinced the model sends hidden messages intended only for them. These descriptions are not three inevitable rungs of the same ladder.

We can have an intense passion without a disorder. We can use a tool compulsively without psychotic symptoms. We can have psychotic symptoms without prolonged use of technology. Putting all of these under the label “AI is driving us mad” would be simultaneously alarmist, clinically imprecise, and too vague to prevent anything.

Psychosis refers to a set of symptoms in which contact with and assessment of reality may be impaired, including delusional beliefs, hallucinations, and disorganized thinking or behavior. It is not synonymous with schizophrenia or with every false opinion. It can arise in different contexts with multiple factors; sleep deprivation, some substances, medications, and other conditions can contribute. Assessment belongs to professionals. [12]

An LLM’s “hallucination,” by contrast, is a technical term used for certain ungrounded or false outputs. It does not demonstrate that the model has hallucinations in the clinical sense. Similarity of words must not lead us to assume similarity of inner experience.

Equally important: an extravagant idea is not a symptom in itself. An unusual scientific hypothesis, a religious belief, or an artistic metaphor must be understood in context. We do not diagnose people by how familiar the content of their ideas is to us.

For this book’s analysis, three questions are more useful than an immediate label. How certain is the person? What could change their mind? What consequences does the belief have for their life and decisions?

Mara can say: “I think I have an important idea; I have not managed to test it yet.” She may be wrong, but she preserves its provisional status. The situation becomes more problematic epistemically if she says: “Every negative test proves the evaluation method is incapable of understanding the theory.” This statement alone still does not give us a clinical diagnosis. It does, however, reveal a relationship with evidence that blocks correction.

A clinically concerning change calls for a broader assessment: the intensity of beliefs, the relationship with reality, sleep, functioning, distress, and medical context. The book does not offer an algorithm for diagnosing a colleague who seems overly enthusiastic.

Pierre and colleagues describe a 26-year-old woman with no history of psychosis or mania who developed delusional beliefs during immersive chatbot use. Conversation logs indicated validation of beliefs related to communicating with a deceased brother. The context included significant sleep deprivation, other psychiatric history, and prescribed stimulant treatment. Hospitalization was necessary. The authors discuss both the chatbot’s possible amplifying role and confounding factors; a later recurrence complicates the causal explanation. One case does not establish the phenomenon’s frequency or prove that technology was the sole cause. [13]

This account calls for two simultaneous responses. First: we do not minimize suffering merely because solid epidemiology is not yet available. Second: we do not turn a complex case into a rule about all users.

In everyday speech, we sometimes say “I am obsessed with the project” with pride. Clinically, matters are more precise and more varied. In this book, we will speak of use that is difficult to control or continues despite consequences when describing behavior, without claiming to have identified a standardized disorder.

The number of hours is information, not a verdict. Four hours of planned project work can mean something different from four hours in which a person repeatedly tries to obtain reassurance that nothing bad will happen. The ability to stop, the purpose, the consequences, and how the rest of life unfolds all matter.

An answer that soothes someone for a few minutes can be useful. But in a hypothetical scenario of repeatedly seeking certainty, each reassurance can create the need for another check. Establishing the effects and the appropriate intervention in a real case requires clinical assessment; the analogy of a button pressed again is not enough.

Intellectual independence does not mean evaluating ourselves alone in every state. We can be highly competent in a field and still need help when sleep, stress, or distress affects our lives. A conversation with a professional is not a verdict on the value of our ideas.

This chapter’s most important separation is between the person and the belief. We can treat the person with dignity and care without affirming an ungrounded explanation. We can take distress seriously without adopting the story that accompanies it. A well-designed conversational system should be able to make the same distinction.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Case report includes confounding factors and recurrence, not incidence or sole causation.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
